lines.text: In seventeen nineteen, two brothers had a Mughal emperor dragged from his palace,
blinded and killed.
No nobles had ever done that to an emperor before.
And within a single year,
four different men sat on the Mughal throne.
How did the greatest empire in the world
become a prize to be handed out?
To see how, go back twelve years, to seventeen oh seven.
The emperor Aurangzeb had ruled for nearly fifty years.
When he died, he left three sons, one empire,
and no agreed heir.
So the princes did what Mughal princes had always done.
They fought.
A Mughal throne was never simply inherited. It had to be won.
The oldest, Prince Muazzam, was about sixty-three.
He was no young warrior,
but he won.
His brother Azam fell in battle that same year,
and his brother Kam Bakhsh died fighting him two years later.
The old prince took the throne as Bahadur Shah the First.
He had won the war.
Now he had to hold the empire together.
His answer was simple: make peace with everyone.
Shahu, the young Maratha prince held captive at the Mughal court,
was set free and sent home.
The Rajput kings were confirmed in their lands.
Only in the Punjab did he send his armies,
against the Sikh leader, Banda Bahadur.
At court, he handed out titles and rewards to keep every faction happy.
So the historian Khafi Khan gave him a nickname:
Shah-i-Bekhabar.
The unaware king.
But the man who made peace with everyone
left no plan for who came next.
In February seventeen twelve, Bahadur Shah died.
His four sons went to war, just as he had.
The winner was Jahandar Shah.
But the real power stood beside the throne.
His chief minister, Zulfikar Khan, ran the empire.
Jahandar Shah held the crown. Zulfikar Khan held the keys.
Zulfikar needed money fast,
so he leaned on izara, revenue farming,
where the right to collect a district's taxes went to whoever bid the most.
It brought in cash quickly, but it could squeeze the peasants hard.
Jahandar Shah also abolished the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims.
But his reign would last less than a year,
because in the east, his nephew was raising an army.
His name was Farrukhsiyar,
and he had two powerful allies.
The Sayyid brothers.
Nobles from an old family of soldiers, with armies of their own.
Abdullah Khan, also called Hassan Ali,
and his younger brother, Hussain Ali.
With their armies behind him, Farrukhsiyar marched on Delhi.
In seventeen thirteen, Jahandar Shah lost the throne, and his life.
The brothers took the top jobs.
One became chief minister. The other commanded the army.
Farrukhsiyar wore the crown, but the brothers held the government.
Farrukhsiyar abolished the jizya again, and the pilgrimage tax too.
And in seventeen seventeen, he signed royal orders called farmans,
letting the English East India Company trade in Bengal without paying customs duty.
It looked like a small favour. But that trade would one day help the Company take Bengal itself.
Farrukhsiyar thought the brothers worked for him.
He was about to learn the opposite.
For six years, he plotted to get rid of them,
turning one noble after another against the brothers.
The brothers grew suspicious, and afraid.
But the brothers struck first.
Hussain Ali marched north from the Deccan,
and with him, according to the historian Ahir, came Maratha troops sent by the Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath.
In February seventeen nineteen, they seized the palace.
Farrukhsiyar was dragged out, blinded, and locked away.
Within weeks, he was killed in prison.
No Mughal emperor had ever been killed by his own nobles before.
From now on, everyone knew the truth.
The throne belonged to whoever held the army.
So the brothers chose the next emperor themselves.
First, a young prince, Rafi-ud-Darajat.
He reigned for just over three months.
When he died, his older brother was crowned as Shah Jahan the Second.
He lasted about three months too.
So the brothers needed a third puppet.
They chose a seventeen-year-old prince, Raushan Akhtar.
In September seventeen nineteen, he was crowned as Muhammad Shah.
Four men on the throne in one year,
and every one of them owed it to the same two brothers.
The brothers thought a teenager would be easy to control.
They were wrong.
Muhammad Shah waited, and quietly found allies.
The most important was Nizam-ul-Mulk,
a powerful noble with his own army in the Deccan.
Together, they moved against the brothers.
In seventeen twenty, Hussain Ali was murdered on the march.
Weeks later, Abdullah Khan was beaten in battle and taken prisoner.
He died in prison in seventeen twenty-two, poisoned.
The kingmakers were gone.
But the damage was done.
Once nobles could make and break emperors,
the emperor stopped being the centre of everything.
Every governor and every general started building power of his own.
In the years that followed, governors in the Deccan, Awadh and Bengal began to rule like kings.
The historian Sidney Owen put it bluntly.
Bahadur Shah the First, he wrote, was the last emperor of whom anything favourable can be said.
A harsh verdict, on every emperor who came after him.
The empire did not fall in one battle.
It fell when its throne became a prize that anyone with an army could give away.
Muhammad Shah would rule for twenty-nine years.
But in seventeen thirty-nine,
a king from Persia was coming for his throne.
